en: To accept or agree to something reluctantly but without protest
hook: ACQUIESCE: 'ACQUI-YES', saying a quiet yes.
story: Acquiesce. Nadia wanted to celebrate her twentieth birthday at a rooftop restaurant with her friends. Her parents insisted on a family dinner at home with every aunt and uncle. She argued. They insisted. Finally she sighed, said, "Fine," and helped her mother cook. She was not happy, but she did not fight. She acquiesced: accepted something reluctantly, without protest. Think of a quiet, unhappy yes. To acquiesce is to give in silently.

gre.s: Although she privately opposed the merger, the director chose to ____ rather than risk a damaging public battle with the board.
gre.clue: rather than risk a damaging public battle

en: Clever or skillful in using the hands or mind
hook: ADROIT: 'a-DROIT' (French for right-handed), skillful.
story: Adroit. The two business partners were shouting at each other across the table, ready to destroy their company. Then their mediator, an elderly woman with a soft voice, asked three clever questions, reframed their dispute, and proposed a deal that gave each of them something they wanted. Twenty minutes later, they were shaking hands. She was adroit: clever and skilful, especially in handling difficult situations. Adroit in French means right-handed, skilled. Synonyms: deft, dexterous.

gre.s: An ____ politician, she managed to satisfy both factions of her party without alienating the voters in the middle.
gre.clue: managed to satisfy both factions of her party

en: To make changes in order to improve or correct
hook: AMEND: MEND something to make it better.
story: Amend. When students protested that the new university rule unfairly punished poor students, the administration listened. Within a month, they amended the rule, adding scholarships and fee waivers. Rafi did the same with his statement of purpose: after his mentor's feedback, he amended it four times, fixing errors and strengthening examples. To amend is to change something to improve or correct it. To make amends means to repair harm you have done.

gre.s: Faced with mounting evidence of its flaws, the legislature voted to ____ the law rather than repeal it entirely.
gre.clue: rather than repeal it entirely

en: Hostility or strong dislike
hook: ANIMUS: like an ANIMAL's growl toward an enemy.
story: Animus. Two coaching centres stood on opposite sides of the same street in Farmgate. Each tore down the other's posters at night, spread rumours about the other's teachers, and offered students free gifts to switch sides. Their owners had once been business partners, and now they could not stand to see each other. Their animus was obvious to everyone: strong hostility or ill will. Synonyms: animosity, antipathy, enmity.

gre.s: Although the critic insisted that his review was purely professional, his evident ____ toward the author suggested a personal grudge.
gre.clue: suggested a personal grudge

en: A person who defends a controversial idea, person, or cause
hook: GRE trick: an APOLOGIST doesn't apologize — he DEFENDS.
story: Apologist. Even after historians proved that a cruel dictator had imprisoned thousands of innocent people, a few commentators still appeared on TV to defend him. "He brought order," they said. "He built roads." They were his apologists: people who defend a controversial person, idea, or cause. An apologist does not apologize; that is a classic GRE trap. The word comes from the Greek apologia, a formal speech in defence.

gre.s: Even his most loyal ____ struggled to justify the general's brutal treatment of civilians.
gre.clue: struggled to justify

en: Sharply severe or critical; also, causing skin tissue to contract
hook: ASTRINGENT: like a STRINGENT, tight squeeze, harsh.
story: Astringent. Arif sent his first novel manuscript to a famous editor. It came back three weeks later with comments in every margin: "Weak." "Lazy." "Cut this." "Why does this exist?" Not one kind word. Arif felt as if his skin had been scrubbed raw. The editor's comments were astringent: sharply severe and critical. Astringent lotions make skin pores contract and tighten. Astringent words make your whole stomach tighten.

gre.s: The critic's ____ reviews, which spared neither famous names nor beginners, made her the most feared voice in the literary world.
gre.clue: spared neither famous names nor beginners

en: To work jointly with others; to cooperate with an enemy
bn: সহযোগিতা করা; শত্রুর সাথে আঁতাত করা
hook: CO-LABOR-ATE: LABOR together.
story: Collaborate. For their final research project, Mitu and Sara decided to collaborate. Mitu was brilliant with data; Sara was a beautiful writer. Mitu ran the analysis while Sara turned the numbers into a clear, convincing story. They won first prize at the national conference. To collaborate is to work jointly with others. Co means together, labor means work. Historically, it can also mean to cooperate traitorously with an enemy occupying your country.

gre.s: Scientists from rival nations agreed to ____ on the project, pooling their data in the hope of an earlier breakthrough.
gre.clue: pooling their data

en: Having enough skill or knowledge to do something successfully
hook: COMPETENT: able to COMPETE.
story: Competent. Tanvir is not the most brilliant programmer in his office. He does not invent clever tricks or win hackathons. But every task he takes on gets done correctly, on time, and without bugs. His manager trusts him with anything. He is competent: having enough skill or knowledge to do something successfully. A competent doctor may not be famous, but you can trust her with your life. Competence is quiet reliability.

gre.s: Although not brilliant, the new manager proved thoroughly ____, handling every crisis calmly and efficiently.
gre.clue: handling every crisis calmly and efficiently

en: To have a mutual relationship in which one thing affects or depends on another
hook: CO-RELATE: RELATED together.
story: Correlate. Researchers surveyed a thousand GRE students. They found that hours of sleep correlated with test scores: students who slept more tended to score higher. But did sleep cause the higher scores? Or were organised students simply better at both sleeping and studying? Correlation is not causation. To correlate is to have a mutual relationship in which one thing changes along with another. GRE arguments love to test this trap.

gre.s: Although rates of the two diseases tend to ____, researchers have found no evidence that one actually causes the other.
gre.clue: researchers have found no evidence that one actually causes the other

en: To mock or express contempt for
hook: DE-RIDE: laughing (ride, from Latin 'ridere') DOWN at someone.
story: Deride. When Rafi announced at a family dinner that he wanted to become a professional chess player, his relatives laughed. "Chess? That is not a job!" They derided his dream: mocked it with contempt. Ten years later, Rafi became a grandmaster, and the same relatives proudly showed his photo to everyone. To deride is to ridicule or express contempt for. De means down, ride from the Latin for laugh: laughing down at someone.

gre.s: Many critics who used to ____ the painter's style as childish now praise it as revolutionary.
gre.clue: now praise it as revolutionary

en: To give orders with authority; to control or determine
hook: DICTATE: what a DICTATOR does.
story: Dictate. Nadia works full time at a bank and studies for the GRE. Her schedule dictates that she can only study from five to seven each morning; there is no other free time. Meanwhile her boss likes to dictate every detail of her work, even the font of her emails. To dictate means to give orders with authority, or to control or determine something. Common sense dictates that you should not drive tired. A dictator dictates everything.

gre.s: The tiny budget seemed to ____ every decision the filmmakers made, from the choice of actors to the length of each scene.
gre.clue: from the choice of actors to the length of each scene

en: Careful in what one says or does, to avoid causing offense or revealing secrets
hook: DISCREET keeps secrets; DISCRETE means separate. Two E's together are 'discreet' — they keep each other's secrets.
story: Discreet. Arif secretly interviewed for a job at another company. He told only one colleague, Joya, and asked her not to mention it. For three weeks, while everyone gossiped about everything, Joya never said a word. Not a hint. When Arif finally announced his new job, everyone was shocked, except her. Joya was discreet: careful about what she says, keeping private matters private. Do not confuse it with discrete, which means separate.

gre.s: The ambassador was chosen for the delicate mission because she was famously ____, never revealing confidential information even to close friends.
gre.clue: never revealing confidential information even to close friends

en: Separated or disconnected from something
hook: GRE trick: DIVORCED FROM reality means disconnected from it.
story: Divorced. During a flood, a minister appeared on TV in a pressed suit and announced that the country had never been more prosperous and that every citizen was well fed. Outside the studio, thousands of people stood in line for a single bag of rice. His speech was completely divorced from reality. On the GRE, divorced from means separated from or disconnected from something. A theory divorced from evidence is just a guess.

gre.s: Critics charged that the economist's elegant models were ____ from reality, ignoring how actual consumers behave.
gre.clue: ignoring how actual consumers behave

en: Believing that a select group is superior and deserves special treatment
hook: ELITIST: thinks only the ELITE matter.
story: Elitist. An exclusive Dhaka club accepted members only from three expensive English-medium schools. Anyone else, however talented, was politely refused. Members joked about "ordinary people" over imported coffee. When a newspaper published the story, readers called the club elitist: believing that a small, privileged group is superior and deserves special treatment. An elitist attitude toward education says only the rich deserve good schools. The opposite is egalitarian.

gre.s: The university's admissions policy was attacked as ____, since it effectively excluded applicants who could not afford expensive private tutoring.
gre.clue: effectively excluded applicants who could not afford expensive private tutoring

en: Making great demands on skill, attention, or effort
bn: কঠোর পরিশ্রম দাবি করে এমন; অতি খুঁতখুঁতে
hook: EXACTING: demands everything to be EXACT.
story: Exacting. Ishita's violin teacher accepted nothing less than perfection. Every note had to be exactly in tune. Every finger had to fall in exactly the right place. One tiny mistake, and the whole piece began again from the first bar. Lessons sometimes lasted three hours. The teacher was exacting: making great demands on skill, attention, and effort. Think: everything must be exact. An exacting task stretches you to your limit.

gre.s: The surgeon's ____ standards, which allowed no margin for error, made her residency program one of the most demanding in the country.
gre.clue: which allowed no margin for error

en: Bewildered; completely confused
hook: FLUMMOXED: sounds like your brain just got FLUMMOXED, flopped and mixed.
story: Flummoxed. The first quant question on Tanvir's GRE showed a strange diagram: overlapping circles, a triangle, and an arrow labelled with a letter he had never seen in a math problem. He stared at it for two full minutes without the faintest idea where to begin. He was flummoxed: bewildered, completely confused. Flummoxed is a fun, informal synonym for befuddled and baffled. Even the word sounds like someone tripping over their own thoughts.

gre.s: The detectives were ____ by the case, as every clue seemed to point in a different direction.
gre.clue: every clue seemed to point in a different direction

en: Producing good or helpful results; productive
hook: FRUITFUL: a tree full of FRUIT.
story: Fruitful. Farhan expected the two-hour project meeting to be a waste of time, as usual. Instead, the team solved three long-standing problems, agreed on a budget, assigned every task, and planned the product launch. Everyone left energised. The meeting had been fruitful: producing good, helpful results. Picture a tree heavy with fruit. A fruitful discussion leads somewhere; a fruitless one wastes everyone's time.

gre.s: After decades of ____ research that yielded dozens of important discoveries, the laboratory was closed for lack of funding.
gre.clue: that yielded dozens of important discoveries

en: Existing from birth; natural
hook: IN-BORN: BORN INside you.
story: Inborn. At four years old, Sara's little brother heard a song on the radio and immediately played it on the family harmonium, without ever having had a lesson. By six he was composing his own tunes. Nobody in the family played music. His talent seemed inborn: existing naturally from birth. Inborn is a synonym of innate. Some abilities are inborn; most skills, like GRE vocabulary, are learned through practice.

gre.s: Linguists debate whether the capacity for grammar is ____ or acquired entirely through exposure to language in early childhood.
gre.clue: or acquired entirely through exposure

en: A person with expert knowledge in many subjects
hook: POLY = many, MATH = learning. Learned in many things.
story: Polymath. Rabindranath Tagore wrote poetry, novels, and plays, composed over two thousand songs, painted thousands of pictures, founded a university, and debated science with Einstein. Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa, designed flying machines, and studied human anatomy. Both were polymaths: people with expert knowledge in many different fields. Poly means many, math means learning. A polymath does not just dabble; they master.

gre.s: A true ____, she published influential papers in physics, composed music, and wrote two acclaimed novels.
gre.clue: published influential papers in physics, composed music, and wrote two acclaimed novels

en: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily
hook: RETICENT: keeps words RETAINED, held back.
story: Reticent. Every Victory Day, students visit an old freedom fighter in Imran's neighbourhood and ask about the war. He smiles quietly, offers them tea, and says only, "It was hard. Many friends did not come back." Then he changes the subject to cricket. He never shares the details. He is reticent: not revealing his thoughts or feelings readily. Think: he retains his words. Careful: reticent does not mean reluctant, though people often confuse them.

gre.s: Usually ____ about her personal life, the actress surprised interviewers by speaking openly about her childhood.
gre.clue: surprised interviewers by speaking openly

en: Strict, precise, and exacting
hook: STRINGENT: tied up with tight STRINGS.
story: Stringent. To get into her dream university, Mitu needed a GRE score of 325, a near-perfect academic record, three strong recommendation letters, a research publication, and an interview. Only four percent of applicants were accepted. Its admission requirements were stringent: strict, precise, and demanding. Picture rules tied up with tight strings. Stringent safety laws protect factory workers. Stringent standards keep quality high.

gre.s: Because the drug's side effects were potentially severe, regulators imposed ____ testing requirements before approving it.
gre.clue: potentially severe

en: Prepared to obey others without question; excessively submissive
hook: SUB-SERVIENT: a SERVANT, below (sub) everyone.
story: Subservient. At every meeting, the director's assistant nodded at every sentence. When the director said the project was brilliant, he agreed. When the director changed his mind ten minutes later, he agreed again. He fetched coffee unasked and never once offered his own opinion. Colleagues called him a shadow. He was subservient: ready to obey without question, excessively submissive. Sub means under; a servant ranks under everyone. Synonyms: servile, obsequious.

gre.s: Critics charged that the newspaper had become ____ to the government, printing official statements without ever questioning them.
gre.clue: printing official statements without ever questioning them

en: Kept secret, especially because it would not be approved of
hook: SURREPTITIOUS: SURE-REPTILE-ish, sneaking like a lizard.
story: Surreptitious. During a boring two-hour lecture, Rafi grew hungry. Every time the professor turned to the whiteboard, he took a quick bite of the sandwich hidden behind his notebook, then chewed silently with a serious face. Nobody noticed, until the professor turned around and asked what he was eating. His snacking had been surreptitious: done secretly, because it would not be approved. Synonyms: furtive, clandestine, stealthy.

gre.s: The spy took ____ photographs of the documents, hiding the tiny camera in the frame of his glasses.
gre.clue: hiding the tiny camera in the frame of his glasses

en: Tempting, but out of reach
hook: TANTALIZING: from TANTALUS, punished with fruit and water just out of reach forever.
story: Tantalizing. During Ramadan, two hours before iftar, the smell of frying beguni and haleem drifted up from Lamia's kitchen. Her stomach growled. The plates were right there on the table, but she could not touch a single bite until sunset. The smell was tantalizing: tempting, yet out of reach. In Greek myth, Tantalus was punished to stand in water that drained away whenever he tried to drink. Tantalizing promises always stay just beyond your grasp.

gre.s: The archaeologists found ____ hints of a lost city, fragments of pottery and a single carved stone, but the site itself has never been located.
gre.clue: but the site itself has never been located

en: Equivalent in seriousness or effect to
hook: TANTAMOUNT: amounts to the same AMOUNT.
story: Tantamount. During the final exam, Zayan saw his best friend copying answers from a hidden phone. He said nothing, and later the friend was caught. The teacher turned to Zayan. "You saw it and stayed silent? That is tantamount to helping him cheat." Tantamount means equivalent in seriousness or effect. It usually describes something bad. Refusing to answer a question can be tantamount to admitting guilt.

gre.s: The senator argued that cutting the program's funding was ____ to abolishing it, since it could not operate on a smaller budget.
gre.clue: since it could not operate on a smaller budget

en: A state of physical or mental inactivity; lethargy
hook: TORPOR: like a TORPEDO that never launched, just sits there.
story: Torpor. After the enormous Eid lunch, the whole family sank into a deep torpor. Uncles lay on sofas, too heavy to talk. Aunties dozed with their eyes half open. The children, who had been running all morning, lay still on mattresses. Even the ceiling fan seemed slower. Torpor is a state of physical or mental inactivity, sluggishness. Some animals enter torpor in winter to save energy. Synonyms: lethargy, inertia, lassitude.

gre.s: The new manager's energy shook the department out of its long ____, and projects that had stalled for years were suddenly completed.
gre.clue: projects that had stalled for years

en: Vigorously effective and sharply clear in expression
hook: TRENCHANT: cuts like a sharp blade digging a TRENCH.
story: Trenchant. In a column of just three sentences, the journalist exposed every flaw in the government's new transport policy: who would pay, who would lose, and why it would fail. Readers said it cut straight to the heart of the issue, like a blade. Her analysis was trenchant: vigorously effective and sharply clear in expression. Picture a sharp blade digging a trench. A trenchant critic does not waste words.

gre.s: The committee was persuaded by the analyst's ____ critique, which exposed the plan's fatal flaws in just a few incisive paragraphs.
gre.clue: in just a few incisive paragraphs

en: Offense or annoyance
hook: UMBRAGE: you take UMBRAGE and go sit in the shade (umbra) to sulk.
story: Umbrage. At dinner, Nadia tasted her uncle's new fish curry and said, "It is very interesting." She meant it kindly. Her uncle put down his spoon, took umbrage, and did not speak to her for the rest of the evening. To take umbrage is to feel offended or annoyed. The word comes from the Latin umbra, meaning shade or shadow, like a dark cloud of resentment settling over someone.

gre.s: The ambassador took ____ at the host's offhand joke about her country, and relations remained frosty for months.
gre.clue: relations remained frosty for months

en: Able to adapt to many different functions or activities
hook: VERSATILE: works in every VERSE, every situation.
story: Versatile. Arif is the most valuable player in his cricket club. He bowls spin, opens the batting, fields brilliantly, and when the wicketkeeper is injured, he takes the gloves. In one match he did all four. His coach calls him a Swiss Army knife. He is versatile: able to adapt to many different functions or activities. A versatile tool serves many purposes; a versatile actor plays heroes, villains, and comedians.

gre.s: The ____ actor, equally convincing as a villain, a comic sidekick, or a tragic hero, has worked in nearly every genre.
gre.clue: equally convincing as a villain, a comic sidekick, or a tragic hero

en: Difficult to control because of unpredictable or disobedient behavior
hook: WAYWARD: going AWAY from the right path.
story: Wayward. At sixteen, Tanvir's cousin began skipping school, staying out until two in the morning, and ignoring every rule his parents set. Teachers called his home weekly. His grandmother prayed for him every night. Years later, he became a social worker who helps other troubled teenagers. As a boy, he was wayward: difficult to control because of unpredictable or disobedient behaviour. Think: going away from the right path. A wayward kite drifts wherever the wind blows.

gre.s: The novel follows a ____ teenager who drifts from one reckless adventure to another before finally finding purpose.
gre.clue: drifts from one reckless adventure to another
